that is used in Eqs. (3) and (4). Fig. 10 shows that runoff coefﬁcients higher than 0.2

average runoff coefﬁcient of watersheds smaller than 10 km2 is 0.9, which results in a
CCR of only 1.25 considering Eq. (3) and using the rainfall and crop data of the
Amrich jessr. Chahbani (1996) proposed a maximum CCR of 3 and 5 if the average
annual precipitation is 150–250 and 100–150 mm, respectively. In case the average
annual precipitation is below 100 mm, he stated that the CCR should be lower than
10. According to Eq. (3) and taking into account the CCR values proposed by
Chahbani (1996), an average annual runoff coefﬁcient of 0.33–0.6 is needed to attain
an annual water amount of 500 mm for crop production.

runoff coefﬁcients that are used. Runoff generation depends on rainfall intensity and
inﬁltration rate, both of which showing a large spatial and temporal variability,
especially in arid regions with non homogeneous soils due to sealing and rock
fragments. The measured inﬁltration rates in this study correspond well with
literature values but further research is needed on different sites in order to obtain

targeting_gate.verbatim_anchor:
The simulation of potential wetland distribution can indicate latent areas for wetland restoration. 
However, wetland loss in China is greatly influenced by human activities, especially encroachment 
of agriculture and expansion of built-up land (Mao et al. 2018a). Overlaying the results of this study 
with those of the China_LUCC for 2020 showed that 8795.5 km2 of potential wetlands in China 
were anthropogenically occupied and unsuitable for wetland restoration. The second national wet­
land resources survey also shows that infrastructure occupation has become one of the five major 
threat factors affecting the change in wetlands in China, and it has permanent effects. Therefore, 
when considering wetland restoration, the first step is to mask off the existing built-up land area 
from the results.
targeting_gate.rationale: Actual restoration targeting overlays potential wetland predictions with current land cover, masks built-up land, and selects convertible covers (PDF17–18). Distinguish occurrence predictors from this final implementation gate.
